You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 6 of 12.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6).
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6).
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (S1-S6).
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (S1-S6).
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (S1-S6).
    *   Piezo properties: $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $I_p \approx 12\mu\text{A}$ peak, $f = 100\text{Hz}$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx 0.76\text{V}$. This is quite low, meaning we need a voltage boost.

    *   The best performing topology so far is `sshi_fbr` (score 79.31).
    *   It uses a SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) stage: $L_1$ and $S_1$ controlled by $G_1$ to invert the piezo voltage.
    *   Then it uses a Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR) (D1-D4).
    *   Storage capacitor $C_{out}$ and Zener clamp $D_z$.
    *   Performance: 5/6 conditions passed.
    *   Failure: $v_{pp}$ on S3 (strong excitation, light load) is 61.1 mV, which exceeds the 50 mV limit.
    *   S3 conditions: $I_p = 40\mu\text{A}$, $R_L = 22\text{k}\Omega$.

    *   In `sshi_fbr`, the energy is delivered in bursts from the inductor/piezo system into $C_{out}$.
    *   S3 has a strong excitation (high $I_p$) and a light load (high $R_L$).
    *   The ripple $v_{pp}$ in $C_{out}$ is $\Delta V \approx \frac{I_{charge} \cdot \Delta t}{C_{out}}$.
    *   Wait, the current delivered to $C_{out}$ is higher in S3, and the load current is lower. If $C_{out}$ is too small, the voltage spikes are too large. If $C_{out}$ is too large, startup $t_{up}$ might fail.
    *   In `sshi_fbr`, $C_{out}$ was tuned to $209\text{nF}$.
    *   For S3, $v_{pp} = 61\text{mV}$. To reduce this to $50\text{mV}$, we need a larger $C_{out}$.
    *   However, we need to check if increasing $C_{out}$ will break the $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ requirement for other conditions (especially S4 - weakest excitation).
    *   In `sshi_fbr`, $t_{up}$ for S4 is $0.119\text{s}$, which is well within the $0.4\text{s}$ limit.
    *   So, simply increasing $C_{out}$ in the `sshi_fbr` topology should work. But the evolution strategy already tried to optimize $C_{out}$. If the best $C_{out}$ for S1, S2, S4, S5, S6 was $209\text{nF}$ and that's what it chose, maybe there's a trade-off.
    *   Wait, looking at the `sshi_fbr` results, it passed $t_{up}$ for all. The only fail was S3 ripple. This suggests the optimizer might have been limited or hit a local minimum. But $C_{out}$ can go up to $47\mu\text{F}$. $209\text{nF}$ is very small.

    *   Why was $C_{out}$ so small in `sshi_fbr`?
    *   Maybe to satisfy the "settled" ($dv \le 0.02\text{V}$) condition?
    *   Wait, $dv$ is the change in mean output between the last two windows (0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s).
    *   If $C_{out}$ is too large, the voltage takes longer to reach steady state, and $dv$ might be too high.
    *   Let's check the `sshi_fbr_L_filter` results: $C_{out}$ was $1\mu\text{F}$, and it failed "settled" and "startup" for S4, S5, S6. This confirms the trade-off: larger $C_{out} \rightarrow$ slower startup and slower settling.

    *   Current `sshi_fbr` (c0042): $C_{out} = 209\text{nF}$. S3 ripple = $61\text{mV}$.
    *   Target S3 ripple: $50\text{mV}$.
    *   Approximate $C_{out}$ needed: $209\text{nF} \cdot (61/50) \approx 254\text{nF}$.
    *   Since $t_{up}$ for S4 is $0.119\text{s}$ and $dv$ for S4 was "ok", there is room to increase $C_{out}$ slightly.

    *   If the optimizer failed to find a slightly larger $C_{out}$ that satisfies everything in the `sshi_fbr` topology, maybe we need a different way to filter the ripple without increasing the overall time constant too much.
    *   The `sshi_fbr_L_filter` tried adding an inductor $L_2$ between the rectifier and $C_{out}$. This created a second-order filter. However, it failed significantly on startup and settling. This is likely because $L_2$ and $C_{out}$ together create a very slow response.

    *   Is there a way to improve the `sshi_fbr` (FBR + SSHI) without just increasing $C_{out}$?
    *   The FBR (Full Bridge Rectifier) has two diode drops. $\text{DSCH} \approx 0.25\text{V}$. Total drop $\approx 0.5\text{V}$.
    *   SSHI helps by flipping the voltage, but the rectifier still takes a toll.
    *   What if we replace the FBR with a synchronous rectifier? (But we only have 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches).
    *   We already used 1 SYNC for the SSHI inversion. We have 1 SYNC left.
    *   A synchronous rectifier would need more switches.

    *   Let's look at the topology again.
    *   The current `sshi_fbr` is:
        Piezo $\rightarrow$ SSHI (L1, S1) $\rightarrow$ FBR (D1-D4) $\rightarrow$ Cout.
    *   Can we use a different rectifier?
    *   A half-bridge rectifier would have fewer diode drops but only use half the energy.
    *   What about a voltage doubler? The reference design failed, but that was a simple FBR. SSHI + Doubler might be powerful.
    *   Wait, the `sshi_dual_doubler` failed the screen.

    *   The `sshi_fbr` is very close. The only issue is the S3 ripple.
    *   S3 is the "strong excitation, light load" case.
    *   High $I_p \rightarrow$ more charge per cycle $\rightarrow$ higher ripple $\Delta V = Q/C_{out}$.
    *   Light load ($R_L = 22\text{k}\Omega$) $\rightarrow$ lower average current $\rightarrow$ higher steady-state voltage.
    *   If we increase $C_{out}$, the ripple $\Delta V$ decreases.
    *   The limiting factor for increasing $C_{out}$ is the "settled" ($dv$) and "startup" ($t_{up}$) conditions.
    *   $dv = |\text{mean}(0.7\text{-}0.8) - \text{mean}(0.6\text{-}0.7)|$.
    *   If $C_{out}$ is too large, the voltage rises slowly.
    *   But in `sshi_fbr`, the $t_{up}$ for S4 (worst case) was $0.119\text{s}$, and the limit is $0.4\text{s}$. This is a huge margin!
    *   Even if we increase $C_{out}$ by $10\text{x}$ (to $2\mu\text{F}$), $t_{up}$ would still be around $1.2\text{s}$? No, $t_{up}$ is the time to reach $1.8\text{V}$.
    *   Let's reconsider the `sshi_fbr_L_filter`. It used $C_{out} = 1\mu\text{F}$ and $L_2 = 4.7\text{mH}$. This $L_2$ is the problem. $L_2$ slows down the charging current significantly.
    *   If we remove $L_2$ and just use a larger $C_{out}$ in the `sshi_fbr` topology, it should work.

    *   Wait, if the evolution strategy already explored `sshi_fbr` and didn't find a solution, it means that for the values of $C_{out}$ it tried, it couldn't satisfy both the S3 ripple and the "settled" condition.
    *   Let's look at the "settled" condition again: $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   In a simple RC circuit, $V(t) = V_{\infty}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$.
    *   The difference between the means of two $0.1\text{s}$ windows at the end of $0.8\text{s}$:
        Window 1: $0.6\text{s}$ to $0.7\text{s}$.
        Window 2: $0.7\text{s}$ to $0.8\text{s}$.
    *   For $C_{out} = 209\text{nF}$ and $R_L = 10\text{k}\Omega$, $\tau = R_L C_{out} \approx 2.1\text{ms}$.
    *   The system should be completely settled. Why did `sshi_fbr_L_filter` fail "settled" with $C_{out} = 1\mu\text{F}$?
    *   Because it had $L_2 = 4.7\text{mH}$. The time constant of an LC filter is much different, and the charging current was limited by $L_2$.
    *   So, the "settled" failure in `sshi_fbr_L_filter` was caused by $L_2$, not by $C_{out}$.

    *   If `sshi_fbr` is failing S3 ripple, and the optimizer couldn't fix it, why?
    *   Let's look at the S3 ripple: $61.1\text{mV}$. Target: $50\text{mV}$.
    *   Wait, if $C_{out} = 209\text{nF}$ gave $61\text{mV}$, then $C_{out} = 300\text{nF}$ should give $\approx 42\text{mV}$.
    *   Is it possible the optimizer was trying to minimize $v_{max}$ or something?
    *   No, $v_{max}$ for S3 was $3.39\text{V}$, which is well below $3.6\text{V}$.
    *   Maybe the optimizer tried $C_{out}$ values that were too large and failed the $dv$ or $t_{up}$ on other conditions?
    *   But S4 $t_{up}$ was $0.119\text{s}$. Even with $C_{out} = 1\mu\text{F}$, $t_{up}$ should be around $0.5\text{s}$.
    *   Wait, the $t_{up}$ limit is $0.4\text{s}$. If $C_{out}$ is too large, $t_{up}$ might exceed $0.4\text{s}$.

    *   Let's try a slightly different approach. Instead of a full bridge, what if we use a charge pump or a different rectifier to reduce the diode drops?
    *   But the SSHI already provides a significant boost.
    *   What if we use a different storage configuration?
    *   The `sshi_fbr` is:
        ```
        L1: pzp -> n1
        S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl=G1)
        D1: pzp -> out
        D2: pzn -> out
        D3: 0 -> pzp
        D4: 0 -> pzn
        Cout: out -> 0
        Dz: 0 -> out
        ```
